name: Cannabis / CBD for sleep

angle.text: Some users take cannabis or CBD to fall asleep more easily, with the aim of waking up looking more rested and recovering better from training. Clinical evidence for sleep is limited, and appearance outcomes from this use are untested.

summary: Cannabis and cannabidiol are used for sleep onset, but clinical evidence is limited and CBD supplements are not FDA-approved for sleep.
note: CBD products are often mislabeled; FDA has raised liver, drug-interaction and fertility concerns.
currentQuick:
Some people use cannabis products or cannabidiol (CBD) to fall asleep. Wikipedia's CBD article says clinical evidence for sleep benefit is limited, and lists sleepiness as a common effect and insomnia among adverse effects of the approved drug Epidiolex.
Only small trials have been registered, for example a phase 2 study of cannabinoids for insomnia in major depression with 14 participants.
How it works: CBD is a non-intoxicating cannabis constituent whose sleep-related mechanisms remain unestablished in the sources reviewed here. THC is the main intoxicating compound.
Risks and caveats: The FDA has cited possible liver toxicity, drug interactions, effects on mood and alertness, and unknown long-term effects. FDA studies found many CBD products were inaccurately labeled and about half of 147 tested contained THC. Legal status varies widely.
deepLead:
Cannabis and cannabidiol (CBD) are used by some people to help with sleep onset. The only FDA-approved CBD medicine, Epidiolex (2018), is indicated for certain seizure disorders, not sleep .
Wikipedia states that CBD may help with pain, sleep and addiction but that clinical evidence is limited; it lists somnolence as common and insomnia as an adverse effect .

name: Alcohol as sleep aid

angle.text: People drink in the evening to fall asleep faster, and looksmaxxing forums discuss the facial effects of the resulting sleep disruption, such as puffiness and a tired look. Sleep effects are documented in reference sources; the facial effects rest mainly on forum claims.

summary: Using alcohol to fall asleep is common; reference sources describe drowsiness alongside disrupted sleep architecture, and facial effects are mainly a looksmaxxing claim.
note: Alcohol disrupts sleep patterns and can worsen existing sleep problems.
currentQuick:
Some people have a drink to fall asleep. Wikipedia's article on the effects of alcohol says alcohol can cause drowsiness while disrupting sleep architecture, particularly later REM sleep, and that it lowers sleep quality and can worsen existing sleep problems.
In looksmaxxing circles, alcohol is also said to cause facial puffiness; the reference source consulted does not discuss puffiness, though it notes alcohol's dehydrating effect and the flush reaction.
How it works: Alcohol acts as a central nervous system depressant. It reduces release of vasopressin, which Wikipedia links to dehydration after heavy drinking.
Risks and caveats: Disrupted sleep during and after drinking; in people who stop after dependence, lingering sleep disruption is described as a strong predictor of relapse (2007 study cited by Wikipedia).
deepLead:
Using alcohol as a sleep aid means drinking in the evening to fall asleep faster. Wikipedia reports that alcohol can cause drowsiness while disrupting sleep architecture, particularly later REM sleep, and that it lowers sleep quality and can greatly worsen existing sleep problems .
Alcohol also reduces production and release of vasopressin, and dehydration is described as a factor in hangover severity . No published study cited here links alcohol use to facial puffiness; this claim circulates in looksmaxxing communities.

name: Trazodone / prescription sleep meds

angle.text: Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant widely used off-label for insomnia, and it comes up in sleep-optimization discussions as a route to more consistent sleep and a more rested look. It has been studied for insomnia modestly; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: A prescription antidepressant widely used off-label for sleep; evidence for insomnia is modest and there are no appearance studies.
note: Prescription-only; adverse effects include sedation, low blood pressure and rare cardiac and priapism events.
currentQuick:
Trazodone is an antidepressant developed in Italy in the 1960s and approved in the US in 1981. Doctors commonly prescribe it at low doses off-label for insomnia, which is how it enters conversations about sleep as a part of looksmaxxing recovery.
Its place in appearance culture is indirect: the premise is that better sleep supports skin, weight and general looks. No published study has tested trazodone or other prescription sleep medicines for any appearance outcome.
How it works: Trazodone blocks serotonin 5-HT2A receptors and also acts on adrenergic and histamine receptors, with a weak effect on serotonin reuptake. Its sedating action is attributed mainly to these receptor effects rather than to a classic sedative mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects include dry mouth, sedation, headache, orthostatic hypotension, and, rarely, QT prolongation, priapism, mania and liver toxicity. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, and stopping abruptly can cause a discontinuation syndrome.
deepLead:
Trazodone is a prescription antidepressant of the serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor class. It was developed by Angelini Research Laboratories in Italy in the 1960s, marketed in Italy from 1972, and approved by the US FDA in 1981 . Its labelled use is major depressive disorder, but at lower doses it is widely prescribed off-label for insomnia .
In the looksmaxxing and recovery context, trazodone and other prescription sleep medicines are discussed as a medical route to better sleep, on the reasoning that sleep quality influences skin, body composition and overall appearance. No published study has examined trazodone for any appearance outcome.
Systematic reviews, including a Cochrane review, have reported short-term improvements in subjective sleep quality and fewer night-time awakenings, with low-to-moderate quality evidence and no data on long-term use. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline recommended against its use for insomnia .

name: Zolpidem (Ambien)

angle.text: Zolpidem is a prescription sleeping pill that appears in sleep and recovery discussions as a way to get more consistent sleep, which people link to better skin and a less tired face. It is studied for short-term insomnia; appearance effects are untested.

summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill with a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors; no appearance research exists.
note: Controlled substance (US Schedule IV); FDA boxed warning for sleepwalking-type behaviors; tolerance and dependence reported.
currentQuick:
Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic sold as Ambien, first used in Europe in 1988 and approved in the US in 1992. It is prescribed for short-term insomnia.
It appears in looksmaxxing recovery discussion as one prescription route to sleep. No study has tested it for any appearance outcome, and its published research concerns insomnia, memory and brain activity.
How it works: Zolpidem is a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors, binding at the benzodiazepine site. Its half-life in healthy adults is about 2 to 3 hours.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include next-day impairment, memory problems, hallucinations, falls and impaired driving. In 2019 the FDA added a boxed warning about complex sleep behaviors such as sleep-driving. Tolerance and dependence are reported, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.
deepLead:
Zolpidem is a nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic, or Z-drug, sold under brand names including Ambien. It was first used in Europe in 1988 by Synthelabo, approved in the US in 1992, and became available as a generic in 2007 . It is indicated for short-term treatment of insomnia, typically two to six weeks .
In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as a prescription option within sleep optimisation. No published study has examined zolpidem for appearance outcomes.
A 2005 review described it as improving sleep with favourable tolerability when used as labelled , while later regulatory actions, including lowered recommended doses in 2013 and a boxed warning in 2019, addressed next-morning impairment and complex sleep behaviors .

name: DSIP (delta sleep-inducing peptide)

angle.text: DSIP is a research peptide that peptide-focused communities discuss for promoting deep sleep, which they connect to recovery, growth hormone and a rested appearance. Human studies on sleep are small and dating from the 1970s and 80s; appearance use is untested.

summary: A nine-amino-acid research peptide first reported in the 1970s to promote sleep; human evidence is small and old.
note: Not an approved drug in the US; long-term safety has not been established in clinical research.
currentQuick:
DSIP is a nine-amino-acid neuropeptide described in 1970s Swiss research after being isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits. It is sold as a research peptide and discussed online as a way to promote deep sleep.
The human literature consists of small studies from the early 1980s, and findings across animal and human work are described as conflicting. No study has examined it for appearance outcomes.
How it works: How DSIP works is not settled. Its gene and receptor have not been identified, and it is broken down quickly in plasma. Proposed mediators include serotonergic and NMDA-related pathways.
Risks and caveats: Safety and possible side effects of long-term use have not been established in clinical studies. Research peptides sold online are not regulated as approved medicines, so product content is not guaranteed.
deepLead:
Delta sleep-inducing peptide (DSIP), also called emideltide, is a neuropeptide with the amino acid sequence WAGGDASGE. It was reported by a Swiss group in the 1970s, who isolated it from the cerebral venous blood of sleeping rabbits .
In biohacking and looksmaxxing recovery discussion, DSIP is described as a research peptide claimed to promote deep sleep. A small human study from 1981 reported increased sleep after intravenous infusion in six volunteers , but later findings from animal and human work have been described as conflicting .
No published study has examined DSIP for appearance outcomes.

name: Growth hormone peptides at bedtime

angle.text: Users inject GH-releasing peptides such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295 before bed to amplify the sleep-time GH pulse, aiming for better recovery, body composition and skin quality. The timing practice itself has not been tested in studies.

summary: Using GH-releasing peptides such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295 before sleep to boost the night-time GH pulse; no studies test this practice.
note: Unapproved research-peptide use; no studies of the bedtime practice itself.
currentQuick:
Some online users take growth hormone secretagogue peptides, such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, shortly before bed, on the reasoning that this adds to the natural growth hormone pulse that occurs during sleep.
The peptides are a recognised drug class, mainly studied for growth hormone deficiency. No published study has tested the bedtime practice or appearance outcomes from it.
How it works: Growth hormone secretagogues act on the ghrelin receptor or on the GHRH receptor to stimulate pituitary growth hormone release, and many also raise IGF-1. Practitioners say bedtime timing aligns the dose with the body's own nocturnal release.
Risks and caveats: These compounds are not approved for cosmetic use. Many secretagogues also raise prolactin and cortisol. Products sold as research chemicals are unregulated, and no safety data exist for the bedtime practice.
deepLead:
Growth hormone peptides at bedtime refers to the practice of using growth hormone secretagogues, such as ipamorelin and CJC-1295, shortly before sleep. The stated aim is to amplify the pulse of growth hormone that occurs during sleep.
Growth hormone secretagogues are a drug class that stimulate growth hormone secretion by acting on the ghrelin receptor (for example ipamorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and ibutamoren) or on the growth hormone releasing hormone receptor (for example CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin) . Their main approved application is treating growth hormone deficiency .
No published trial has tested the bedtime practice, or appearance outcomes from it, in people without a deficiency.

name: Morning sunlight viewing

angle.text: People get outdoor light soon after waking to set their circadian clock, aiming for better sleep and a more rested look. It builds on established light-therapy research on circadian timing; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

summary: Spending time outdoors soon after waking to anchor the body clock; related to established light-therapy research, with no appearance studies.
note: Looking directly at the sun can harm eyes.
currentQuick:
Morning sunlight viewing is the practice of spending roughly ten to thirty minutes outdoors after waking, on the idea that early light sets the circadian clock and so supports sleep and general well-being.
The underlying idea of timed light exposure is studied in bright light therapy, where morning treatment is used for seasonal depression and circadian sleep disorders. No study has tested the outdoor practice for appearance outcomes.
How it works: Light acts on specialised retinal cells that reset the body's internal clock and suppress melatonin. The effect depends on timing relative to the body's core temperature minimum.
Risks and caveats: Intense light of any kind can harm eyes and skin, and unprotected UV exposure raises skin cancer risk. Light therapy can trigger mania in susceptible people.
deepLead:
Morning sunlight viewing is a lifestyle practice in which people spend roughly ten to thirty minutes outside soon after waking, with the stated aim of anchoring the circadian clock.
The general principle that light resets the body's internal clock is established in light therapy. Wikipedia reports that light suppresses melatonin through light-sensitive retinal cells and that morning treatment has worked best for seasonal affective disorder because early light helps set the circadian rhythm .
No studies were found testing the outdoor practice itself for appearance outcomes.

name: Blue light blocking glasses

angle.text: Users wear amber or tinted glasses in the evening to protect melatonin and fall asleep more easily, which they link to better skin and less puffiness. Small trials have looked at sleep and melatonin; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: Amber or tinted glasses worn in the evening to reduce blue light and protect melatonin; small trials exist, reviews of eye-health claims are mixed.
note: Reviews cited by Grokipedia report limited evidence for eye strain and sleep benefits in general populations.
currentQuick:
Blue light blocking glasses filter part of the blue spectrum (about 400 to 500 nm) emitted by screens and LEDs. In sleep circles, amber-tinted versions are worn in the evening on the idea that blue light suppresses melatonin and delays sleep.
Small trials have tested evening use in teenagers, healthy adults and people with delayed sleep phase disorder. Broader reviews of eye strain and sleep claims are described as mixed.
How it works: Lenses use dye-based tints, commonly amber or yellow, or thin-film interference coatings to absorb or reflect part of the blue wavelengths. The circadian system is most sensitive to blue light, which is the basis for the evening-use rationale.
Risks and caveats: No notable harms are reported for ordinary use. A 2007 paper discussed safety considerations for wearing them in shift workers, who need to stay alert.
deepLead:
Blue light blocking glasses are eyewear designed to filter part of the blue spectrum, typically 400 to 500 nm, from screens, LED lighting and sunlight. Lenses use amber or yellow dye-based tints or interference coatings, and are available with or without prescription .
Proponents of evening use, including users interested in sleep optimisation, say that blue light suppresses melatonin and delays the body clock, so filtering it after dark protects sleep. Small trials have tested this, including studies in teenagers , people with delayed sleep phase disorder  and healthy adults .
Broader assessments differ. Grokipedia reports that Cochrane reviews and the American Academy of Ophthalmology found no clear benefit for eye strain or sleep from blue-light-filtering lenses in general use .

name: Red light at night

angle.text: Sleep-focused communities swap white evening bulbs for red ones to keep melatonin and the body clock undisturbed, aiming for better sleep and a more rested look. The idea follows from light science; this use is untested.

summary: Swapping white evening lights for red ones to protect melatonin; the idea is plausible from light science but untested for this use.
note: Animal studies are mixed on bright red light and melatonin.
currentQuick:
This habit replaces white household lights with red ones in the evening. The reasoning is that blue-ish light affects the body clock most.
No human trial has tested it for sleep or appearance, and the lab findings on red light and melatonin are mixed.
How it works: The circadian system is most responsive to short-wavelength light, so long-wavelength light is proposed to interfere less. Rat studies found bright red light could still suppress melatonin.
Risks and caveats: No direct risks are documented. The main caveat is that the effect on sleep in people has not been studied.
deepLead:
Using red or dim red bulbs instead of white light in the evening is a lighting habit in sleep-focused communities, based on the idea that long-wavelength light disturbs melatonin and the body clock less than white or blue light.
Reference sources describe short-wavelength (blue) light as having the strongest effect on melatonin suppression and circadian timing. Studies on red light itself are few and not specific to this habit: some animal experiments found that bright red light suppressed melatonin in rats, while a study in horses reported that red light allowed a nighttime melatonin rise, and a review of light at night for shift workers noted that long-wavelength light can raise alertness.

name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox

angle.text: Looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities cut screens before bed and take breaks from stimulation to sleep better and stay focused, which feeds into skin, puffiness and energy. The light-and-sleep logic has research support; the dopamine framing is disputed.

summary: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation; the light-and-sleep logic has support, the "dopamine" framing is disputed.
note: Neuroscientists dispute the dopamine-reset explanation.
currentQuick:
A screen curfew stops device use before bed. Dopamine detox goes further and abstains from stimulating activities for a period.
Evening-light research gives the first a basis for sleep; the second has no defined protocol or trials.
How it works: Device light can delay the body clock and melatonin. Dopamine fasting is said to reduce impulsive habits rather than dopamine itself.
Risks and caveats: No direct harms are documented, though extreme versions of dopamine fasting have been criticized by clinicians.
deepLead:
A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are discussed as ways to improve sleep and focus.
Reference sources describe evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs as able to delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality. Dopamine fasting was popularized by psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it targets impulsive behaviours rather than literally lowering dopamine; neuroscientists have criticized the name and the idea of a brain "reset".

name: Consistent sleep schedule

angle.text: Forum posters keep fixed bed and wake times as a free way to support hormones, growth and recovery, with claims of larger growth hormone pulses. It is standard sleep-hygiene advice; trials on looks or height claims do not exist.

summary: Same bed and wake times daily; a standard sleep-hygiene habit, with no trials for looks or height claims.
note: Hormone and height claims in forums are untested.
currentQuick:
Going to bed and waking at the same times each day is basic sleep-hygiene advice and costs nothing.
Sleep research links poor or irregular sleep with metabolic and hormonal changes, but no study tests the practice for appearance.
How it works: It is proposed to keep the body clock and hormone rhythms aligned.
Risks and caveats: No risks are documented. Sleep hygiene alone is not supported as a stand-alone insomnia treatment by a 2021 meta-analysis.
deepLead:
A consistent sleep schedule means going to bed and waking at about the same times every day, including weekends. It is a standard element of sleep-hygiene advice and is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a free way to support hormones, growth and recovery.
Reference sources state that a regular wake time tends to improve sleep, though overall evidence that sleep hygiene alone treats insomnia is weak. Research links irregular sleep patterns and poor sleep quality with obesity-related measures in adolescents and sleep disorders with hormonal and metabolic changes, but these are associational findings and none addresses appearance directly.

name: Bedroom temperature (cold room, 65F)

angle.text: Sleep routines in looksmaxxing and wellness communities keep the bedroom cool, around 65 F, to sleep more deeply and wake looking more rested. Cool rooms appear in sleep-hygiene advice; the specific temperature and appearance link are untested.

summary: Sleeping in a cool room; recommended in sleep-hygiene advice, but the specific 65 F figure is untested here.
note: Sleep hygiene overall has weak evidence as a standalone treatment.
currentQuick:
People keep the bedroom cool, often about 65 F, to sleep better.
Guidance backs a cool sleeping environment generally, but no source reviewed tests a specific temperature or appearance effects.
How it works: Uncomfortable temperatures can disrupt continuous sleep, so a cooler room is meant to reduce disruption.
Risks and caveats: No documented risks beyond personal comfort.
deepLead:
The cold-room habit keeps the bedroom cool, often around 65 F (about 18 C), on the belief that cooler air supports sleep. It is a common item in sleep routines in looksmaxxing and wellness communities.
Sleep-hygiene guidance recommends a quiet, dark and cool sleeping environment and notes that uncomfortable temperatures can disrupt continuous sleep, though reference sources do not rate temperature separately and describe the overall evidence for sleep hygiene as weak.

name: Cooling mattress pad (Eight Sleep)

angle.text: Sleep-optimization communities use temperature-controlled mattress covers to hold a cool sleeping surface through the night, aiming for deeper sleep and better recovery. Users praise the temperature control; no trials examine looks.

summary: An app-connected bed cover that heats and cools; praised for temperature control, subscription-dependent, no looks trials.
note: Many features require a subscription and cloud connection.
currentQuick:
Eight Sleep makes a bed cover that actively heats or cools the sleeping surface and tracks sleep.
Reviewers praise the temperature control; the product has not been tested for appearance outcomes in the sources reviewed.
How it works: The cover circulates temperature-controlled water through the bed and adjusts via an app.
Risks and caveats: A 2025 cloud outage left some units overheating, and most features require a subscription since 2023.
deepLead:
Eight Sleep is an American company founded in 2014 that sells temperature-controlled bedding, notably the Pod smart mattress cover, which actively heats or cools the bed. It is discussed in sleep-optimization communities as a way to hold a cool sleeping surface.
Reviewers have praised its temperature control, though a later review said similar features are available elsewhere for less; since February 2023 most functions require a subscription. No clinical trial reviewed here tests the product for appearance outcomes.

name: Weighted blanket

angle.text: Users sleep under weighted blankets to feel calmer at bedtime and sleep better, which they tie to a more rested appearance. Trials exist mainly in clinical groups with mixed results; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: A heavy blanket for calming pressure at bedtime; trial evidence exists mainly in clinical groups and is mixed.
note: Not advised for infants or very small children; people with breathing problems are advised to consult a clinician.
currentQuick:
A weighted blanket is a quilt filled with pellets, beads or chains that presses evenly on the body. It came out of occupational therapy and became a mainstream consumer product after 2017.
Studies are mostly in autistic, ADHD or psychiatric populations and results are mixed; evidence in healthy adults is limited, and nothing tests it for appearance.
How it works: Proponents say deep pressure calms the nervous system, in a way similar to being hugged. This remains a proposed mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Safety warnings concern infants and small children, and people with respiratory or circulatory conditions. A child's death linked to improper use has been reported.
deepLead:
A weighted blanket is a blanket filled with pellets, glass beads or chains so that it presses evenly on the body, commonly weighing about 5 to 30 pounds (2.3 to 13.6 kg). It is used in occupational therapy for deep pressure stimulation and is sold to consumers as a sleep and anxiety aid. In sleep-focused communities it is discussed as a way to feel calmer at bedtime.
Published research is limited and mixed. A 2020 systematic review described the literature on weighted blankets as sparse, a randomized trial in psychiatric patients with insomnia reported benefit on an insomnia scale, and a randomized crossover trial in autistic children found no significant change in the main sleep measures. Safety concerns are documented for young children and people with respiratory or circulatory conditions.

name: Sleep tracker (Oura / Whoop / Eight Sleep)

angle.text: Looksmaxxing communities use rings, bands and bed covers to monitor sleep, which proponents link to skin, facial puffiness and energy. Trackers are useful for trends, with stage accuracy debated; the appearance link rests on anecdote.

summary: Rings, bands and bed covers that score your sleep, useful as a trend log, shaky on stage accuracy.
note: Subscription fees; sleep-stage accuracy limited vs polysomnography.
currentQuick:
Sleep trackers estimate how long and how well you sleep using motion, heart rate and temperature sensors. Oura (a ring), Whoop (a band) and Eight Sleep (a bed cover) are the names most often mentioned in looksmaxxing communities.
They are discussed as a way to monitor a habit that proponents link to skin and looks. No studies were found testing that link.
How it works: Optical and motion sensors feed proprietary algorithms that output sleep duration, stages and recovery scores.
Risks and caveats: Cited research reports limited accuracy for sleep staging versus polysomnography, ongoing subscription costs, and reports of anxiety over scores.
deepLead:
Consumer sleep trackers are wearable or bed-based devices that estimate sleep duration, sleep stages and related measures such as heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate. Well-known examples include the Oura smart ring, the Whoop strap and the Eight Sleep smart mattress cover. Looksmaxxing communities discuss them as tools for monitoring sleep, which proponents link to skin, facial puffiness and energy.
Oura Health was founded in Finland in 2013 and sells a ring that combines light sensors to track heart rate, HRV, respiration, temperature and sleep, condensing the data into scores from 0 to 100. Whoop, founded in Boston in 2012, sells a screenless band and a subscription that produce daily recovery, strain and sleep scores.
Polysomnography is regarded as the gold standard for measuring sleep, and consumer devices estimate sleep from motion and other sensors using proprietary algorithms. Research cited on Wikipedia reports that they tend to over- or underestimate total sleep time and are limited at staging sleep.

name: Sleep hygiene basics

angle.text: Users follow a dark, cool, quiet and regular sleep routine as a baseline for looking more rested. Sleep hygiene was developed for mild to moderate insomnia; its effect on appearance is untested.

summary: Dark, cool, quiet, regular sleep habits; a sensible baseline, but weak evidence as a stand-alone insomnia fix.
note: Not favored by the AASM as stand-alone insomnia therapy.
currentQuick:
Sleep hygiene is a list of habits meant to help sleep: regular times, a dark, cool, quiet room, and limiting caffeine and alcohol late.
It is a common baseline in looksmaxxing discussion. Reviews describe the evidence for it alone as weak.
How it works: It aims to align behavior and environment with the body's sleep-wake rhythm and reduce arousal at bedtime.
Risks and caveats: Little direct risk is reported; the AASM analysis cautioned that relying on it alone for chronic insomnia can delay effective treatment.
deepLead:
Sleep hygiene is a set of behavioral and environmental practices intended to promote healthy sleep, such as a regular schedule and a dark, cool, quiet bedroom. The concept was developed in the late 1970s to help people with mild to moderate insomnia.
In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as a foundational habit, on the belief that good sleep supports skin, eye area and general appearance.
Reviews describe the evidence that sleep hygiene alone improves sleep as weak and inconclusive, and a 2021 American Academy of Sleep Medicine meta-analysis did not favor it as stand-alone therapy for chronic insomnia.

name: CBT-I

angle.text: People with chronic insomnia use CBT-I, a structured therapy, to restore sleep, and appearance communities connect better sleep with skin, eyes and a less tired face. It is guideline-recommended for insomnia; no studies test looks directly.

summary: The guideline-recommended first-line therapy for chronic insomnia; nothing tested on looks directly.
note: Sleep restriction can cause daytime sleepiness; not suitable for everyone.
currentQuick:
CBT-I is a structured program that changes sleep-related habits and thoughts to treat chronic insomnia. Guidelines such as the American College of Physicians' recommend it first.
Looksmaxxing communities mention it for sleep quality; no studies were found testing effects on appearance.
How it works: It combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy and relaxation to rebuild the association between bed and sleep.
Risks and caveats: Sleep restriction can temporarily cause fatigue and sleepiness, and some conditions such as epilepsy or bipolar disorder call for caution.
deepLead:
Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, multi-component treatment for chronic insomnia that combines techniques such as stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene. It is described as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.
The American College of Physicians (2016) recommends CBT-I as initial treatment for chronic insomnia in adults, and a 2015 meta-analysis reported benefits on diary measures of sleep. Digital versions have been tested in randomized trials.
In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned as the evidence-based option for people whose poor sleep affects appearance; no studies were found linking it to appearance outcomes.

name: Caffeine cutoff (no caffeine after noon)

angle.text: Proponents stop caffeine by noon so it does not interfere with sleep, which they say benefits skin and appearance. The half-life reasoning is plausible; the exact cutoff and the appearance link are untested.

summary: Stop caffeine by noon to protect sleep; plausible given half-life, but the exact cutoff is untested.
note: Individual sensitivity varies widely.
currentQuick:
The rule says to stop caffeine by around noon so it doesn't interfere with sleep.
Caffeine's half-life of about 3-7 hours gives the idea a basis, though no studies were found on the specific noon cutoff.
How it works: Caffeine blocks sleepiness signals and clears slowly, so late doses may still be active at bedtime.
Risks and caveats: Little risk from the habit itself; abrupt reduction by regular users can bring withdrawal effects.
deepLead:
The caffeine cutoff is a habit of stopping caffeine intake by a set time, often noon or early afternoon, to protect sleep. Proponents say better sleep benefits skin and appearance.
Wikipedia reports caffeine's half-life in healthy adults as about 3 to 7 hours, that it can delay or prevent sleep, and that sensitivity varies widely between people.
No studies were found testing a specific noon cutoff or its effects on appearance.

name: Late-night eating cutoff

angle.text: Users stop eating about three hours before bed, aiming for less morning facial puffiness and better sleep. The practice in this form has not been tested.

summary: Stop eating about 3h before bed for less puffiness and better sleep; untested in this form.
note: Meal-timing research is largely observational.
currentQuick:
The habit is to stop eating about three hours before bed.
Communities say it reduces puffiness and aids sleep. No studies were found testing that specific claim, though meal timing is an active research area.
How it works: Proponents say a lighter digestive load at bedtime aids sleep; chrononutrition research links meal timing to circadian rhythms.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms; people with medical conditions affecting blood sugar are generally guided by clinicians on meal timing.
deepLead:
The late-night eating cutoff is the practice of stopping food about three hours before bed. Proponents say it reduces morning facial puffiness and improves sleep.
Research on meal timing falls under chrononutrition, the study of how eating times interact with circadian rhythms. Wikipedia reports that epidemiological studies link late dinners with higher metabolic risk but that causality needs more research.
No studies found testing a three-hour cutoff for puffiness or appearance.

name: Evening hot shower / bath

angle.text: People take a warm shower or bath before bed to fall asleep faster as core temperature drops afterward, and link better sleep with a more rested appearance. Sourcing for this routine is thin; appearance effects are untested.

summary: A warm shower or bath before bed for faster sleep onset; thinly sourced here.
note: Very hot water can cause drowsiness or dizziness.
currentQuick:
The practice is a warm shower or bath in the evening to ease into sleep.
Sources reviewed for this wiki do not test the claim.
How it works: Proponents say the body cools after the bath, signaling sleep.
Risks and caveats: Very hot water can cause drowsiness; the hot tub article treats that as a drowning risk.[1]
deepLead:
The evening hot shower or bath is a pre-bed routine that proponents say promotes sleep onset by relaxing the body and, as it cools afterward, lowering core temperature.
This claim is circulated in sleep and looksmaxxing communities; Wikipedia articles on sleep onset and hot tubs, the pages reviewed for this entry, do not cover it, and the hot tub article notes only that sitting in water above normal body temperature can cause drowsiness, presented as a drowning risk.
Source material for this entry is thin.
